title: Bellwethers: A Baseline Method For Transfer Learning

edges.target: TCA+ transfer component analysis (Nam, Pan, Kim)
edges.ref: [10] J. Nam, S. J. Pan, and S. Kim, "Transfer defect learning," in Proc. ICSE, 2013, pp. 382-391.
edges.evidence: we compare the "bellwether" method [20] against 3 other standard transfer learners: (1) TCA+ [10]; (2) Transfer Naive Bayes [21]; and (3) Value Cognitive Boosting [22]

edges.target: TCA+ defect-prediction result (Nam et al.)
edges.ref: [10] J. Nam, S. J. Pan, and S. Kim, "Transfer defect learning," in Proc. ICSE, 2013, pp. 382-391.
edges.evidence: TCA+ was generally better than the other three methods with an overall W/T/L ratio of 8/3/5 ... this behavior of TCA+ corroborates with previous findings by other researchers [10]

edges.target: Transfer Naive Bayes, TNB (Ma et al.)
edges.ref: [21] Y. Ma, G. Luo, X. Zeng, and A. Chen, "Transfer learning for cross-company software defect prediction," IST, vol. 54, no. 3, pp. 248-256, 2012.
edges.evidence: Issue lifetime dataset: From Figure 11, we see that, in this case, TNB outperforms the other three methods. We note a W/T/L ratio for TNB at 7/0/2

edges.target: Value-Cognitive Boosting with SVM, VCB (Ryu et al.)
edges.ref: [22] D. Ryu, O. Choi, and J. Baik, "Value-cognitive boosting with a support vector machine for cross-project defect prediction," Empir. Softw. Eng.
edges.evidence: We could not use VCB in code smell detection because our datasets had small sample size ... We could not use VCB in effort estimation either because the class variable was continuous

edges.target: Bellwether effect / method, ASE'16 (Krishna, Menzies, Fu)
edges.ref: [20] R. Krishna, T. Menzies, and W. Fu, "Too Much Automation? The Bellwether Effect and Its Implications for Transfer Learning," in ASE'16, 2016.
edges.evidence: This work presents a significant extension to our initial findings on bellwethers [20] ... Our initial work [20] compared bellwethers against two other transfer learners invented by ourselves

edges.target: Random Forests (Breiman)
edges.ref: [134] L. Breiman, "Random forests," Machine learning, pp. 5-32, 2001.
edges.evidence: When a specific transfer learner did not endorse the use of any classification/regression scheme, we used Random Forests

edges.target: Lessmann et al. benchmark endorsing Random Forests
edges.ref: [65] S. Lessmann, B. Baesens, C. Mues, and S. Pietsch, "Benchmarking Classification Models for Software Defect Prediction," IEEE TSE, vol. 34, no. 4
edges.evidence: A comprehensive study on defect prediction was conducted by Lessmann et al. [65]. They endorsed the use of Random Forests [134] for defect prediction over several other methods

edges.target: SMOTE (Chawla et al.)
edges.ref: [136] N. V. Chawla, K. W. Bowyer, L. O. Hall, and W. P. Kegelmeyer, "SMOTE: Synthetic minority over-sampling technique," J. Artif. Intell. Res., vol.
edges.evidence: To overcome the inherent randomness introduced by Random Forests and SMOTE, we use 30 repeated runs ... SMOTE is only applicable for classification problems

edges.target: Pelayo & Dick: SMOTE improves defect prediction
edges.ref: [135] L. Pelayo and S. Dick, "Applying Novel Resampling Strategies To Software Defect Prediction," in NAFIPS 2007, pp. 69-72.
edges.evidence: Pelayo and Dick [135] report that the defect prediction is improved by SMOTE [136]

edges.target: Code-smell datasets, God Class & Feature Envy (Fontana et al.)
edges.ref: [108] F. Arcelli Fontana, M. V. Mantyla, M. Zanoni, and A. Marino, "Comparing and experimenting machine learning techniques for code smell
edges.evidence: They made available their dataset, which we have adapted for our applications in this study ... The code smells repository we use comprises of 22 datasets for two different code smells

edges.target: Fontana et al.: RF best for code smell detection
edges.ref: [108] F. Arcelli Fontana, M. V. Mantyla, M. Zanoni, and A. Marino, "Comparing and experimenting machine learning techniques for code smell
edges.evidence: They endorsed the use of Random Forests [134] for defect prediction over several other methods. This was also true in detecting code smells [108]

edges.target: Qualitas Corpus (Tempero et al.)
edges.ref: [109] E. Tempero, C. Anslow, J. Dietrich, et al., "Qualitas corpus: A curated collection of java code for empirical studies," in APSEC 2010, pp.
edges.evidence: These datasets were generated using the Qualitas Corpus (QC) of systems [109] ... Fontana et al. [108] selected a subset of 74 systems for their analysis

edges.target: Issue lifetime data, 8 GitHub projects (Rees-Jones et al.)
edges.ref: [113] M. Rees-jones, M. Martin, C. College, and T. Menzies, "Better Predictors for Issue Lifetime," pp. 1-8, 2017.
edges.evidence: Figure 4 shows a list of 8 projects used to study issue lifetimes ... It forms a part of an ongoing study on prediction of issue lifetime by Rees-Jones et al. [113]

edges.target: Sticky-issue removal and feature extraction protocol (Rees-Jones et al.)
edges.ref: [113] M. Rees-jones, M. Martin, C. College, and T. Menzies, "Better Predictors for Issue Lifetime," pp. 1-8, 2017.
edges.evidence: As recommended by Rees-Jones et al. [113], we removed these sticky issues from our datasets ... we did similar preprocessing and feature extraction on the raw datasets as suggested by [113]

edges.target: COCOMO effort datasets NASA93, NASA10, COC10/COC05 (Menzies et al.)
edges.ref: [115] T. Menzies, Y. Yang, G. Mathew, B. Boehm, and J. Hihn, "Negative results for software effort estimation," Empirical Software Engineering, pp.
edges.evidence: The data was made available by Menzies et al. [115] who show that this model works better than (or just as well as) other models ... We use 5 datasets shown in Figure 4

edges.target: COC81 dataset and COCOMO ontology (Boehm)
edges.ref: [116] B. W. Boehm et al., Software engineering economics. Prentice-hall Englewood Cliffs (NJ), 1981, vol. 197.
edges.evidence: COC81 is the original data from 1981 COCOMO book [116]. This comes from projects dated from 1970 to 1980 ... The non-proprietary data ... are available at http://tiny.cc/07wvjy

edges.target: AEEEM defect data (D'Ambros et al.)
edges.ref: [128] M. D'Ambros, M. Lanza, and R. Robbes, "Evaluating defect prediction approaches: a benchmark and an extensive comparison," Empir. Softw. Eng.
edges.evidence: The first dataset, AEEEM, was used by [11]. This dataset was gathered by D'Amborse et al. [128], it contains 61 metrics

edges.target: ReLink defect data (Wu et al.)
edges.ref: [129] R. Wu, H. Zhang, S. Kim, and S.-C. Cheung, "ReLink," in Proc. 19th ACM SIGSOFT Symp. / 13th Eur. Conf. Found. Softw. Eng. - SIGSOFT/FSE '11
edges.evidence: The RELINK community data was obtained from work by Wu et al. [129] who used the Understand tool, to measure 26 metrics

edges.target: Apache/Jureczko PROMISE defect data (Jureczko & Madeyski), via SEACRAFT
edges.ref: [133] M. Jureczko and L. Madeyski, "Towards identifying software project clusters with regard to defect prediction," in Proc. PROMISE '10, ACM, 2010
edges.evidence: we explored two other communities of datasets from the SEACRAFT repository. The group of data contains defect measures from several Apache projects. It was gathered by Jureczko et al. [133]

edges.target: XTREE paper describing the Apache defect data (Krishna, Menzies, Layman)
edges.ref: [103] R. Krishna, T. Menzies, and L. Layman, "Less is More: Minimizing Code Reorganization using XTREE," CoRR, vol. abs/1609.03614, 2016.
edges.evidence: Each dataset in the Apache community has several versions. There are a total of 38 different datasets. For more information on this dataset see [103]

edges.target: Scott-Knott ranking (Mittas & Angelis)
edges.ref: [28] N. Mittas and L. Angelis, "Ranking and clustering software cost estimation models through a multiple comparisons algorithm," IEEE Trans.
edges.evidence: To rank these 30 numbers collected as above, we use the Scott-Knott test recommended by Mittas and Angelis [28]

edges.target: Non-parametric bootstrap hypothesis test (Efron & Tibshirani)
edges.ref: [148] B. Efron and R. J. Tibshirani, An introduction to the bootstrap, ser. Mono. Stat. Appl. Probab. London: Chapman and Hall, 1993.
edges.evidence: As for hypothesis test, we use a non-parametric bootstrapping test as endorsed by Efron & Tibshirani [148, p220-223]

edges.target: A12 effect size (Vargha & Delaney)
edges.ref: [155] A. Vargha and H. D. Delaney, "A critique and improvement of the cl common language effect size statistics of mcgraw and wong," J. Educ. Behav.
edges.evidence: A popular effect size test used in SE literature is the A12 test ... It was first proposed by Vargha and Delany [155] ... not a small effect (A12 >= 0.6)

edges.target: Arcuri & Briand guide to statistical tests for randomized algorithms
edges.ref: [151] A. Arcuri and L. Briand, "A practical guide for using statistical tests to assess randomized algorithms in software engineering," in ICSE'11
edges.evidence: A popular effect size test used in SE literature is the A12 test. It has been endorsed by several SE researchers [149], [150], [151], [152], [153], [154]

edges.target: Kocaguneli et al. distributed development (A12 endorsement)
edges.ref: [154] E. Kocaguneli, T. Zimmermann, C. Bird, N. Nagappan, and T. Menzies, "Distributed development considered harmful?" in Proc. ICSE, 2013, pp.
edges.evidence: It has been endorsed by several SE researchers [149], [150], [151], [152], [153], [154]

edges.target: Standardized Accuracy, SA (Shepperd & MacDonell)
edges.ref: [137] M. Shepperd and S. MacDonell, "Evaluating prediction systems in software project estimation," Information and Software Technology, vol. 54, no.
edges.evidence: To evaluate the quality of the learners used for regression, we make use of Standardized Accuracy (SA). The use of SA has been endorsed by several researchers in SE [137], [138]

edges.target: MARP0 baseline / SA endorsement (Langdon et al.)
edges.ref: [138] W. B. Langdon, J. Dolado, F. Sarro, and M. Harman, "Exact mean absolute error of baseline predictor, marp0," Information and Software
edges.evidence: The use of SA has been endorsed by several researchers in SE [137], [138]

edges.target: G-score / harmonic mean of pd and 1-pf; avoid precision (Menzies et al. 'Problems with Precision')
edges.ref: [3] T. Menzies, A. Dekhtyar, J. Distefano, and J. Greenwald, "Problems with Precision: A Response to ...," IEEE TSE, vol. 33, no. 9, pp. 637-640
edges.evidence: we use the the G-Score for combining Pd and Pf. Several authors [3], [144] have previously shown that such a measure is justifiably better than other measures when the test samples have imbalanced distribution

edges.target: Shatnawi: pd/pf-based measure for imbalanced classes
edges.ref: [144] R. Shatnawi, "A quantitative investigation of the acceptable risk levels of object-oriented metrics in open-source systems," IEEE TSE, vol. 36
edges.evidence: Several authors [3], [144] have previously shown that such a measure is justifiably better than other measures when the test samples have imbalanced distribution

edges.target: Ma & Cukic: distance-from-perfect metrics substitute for AUC
edges.ref: [145] Y. Ma and B. Cukic, "Adequate and precise evaluation of quality models in software engineering studies," in PROMISE'07: ICSE Workshops 2007
edges.evidence: Ma and Cukic [145] have shown that other metrics that measure the distance from perfect classification can be substituted for AUC in cases where a ROC curve cannot be generated

edges.target: Kubat & Matwin: negative class effect on metrics
edges.ref: [143] M. Kubat, S. Matwin et al., "Addressing the curse of imbalanced training sets: one-sided selection," in ICML, vol. 97, 1997, pp. 179-186.
edges.evidence: Kubat & Matwin found that the effect of the negative classes ... has a profound impact on the outcome of these metrics. As a remedy, these authors recommend a new evaluation scheme

edges.target: AM-GM-HM inequality (Xia, Xu, Qi)
edges.ref: [146] D.-F. Xia, S.-L. Xu, and F. Qi, "A proof of the arithmetic mean-geometric mean-harmonic mean inequalities," RGMIA research report collection
edges.evidence: in cases where samples tend to take extreme values (such as Pd=0 or Pf=1) harmonic mean provides estimates that are much more stable and also more conservative ... compared to geometric mean [146]

edges.target: Vaux et al.: repeated runs for reliable evidence
edges.ref: [147] D. L. Vaux, F. Fidler, and G. Cumming, "Replicates and repeats - what is the difference and is it significant?" EMBO reports, vol. 13, no. 4
edges.evidence: we use 30 repeated runs, each time with a different random number seed ... Researchers have endorsed the use of repeated runs to gather reliable evidence [147]

edges.target: Whigham et al. baseline-method guidelines
edges.ref: [27] P. A. Whigham, C. A. Owen, and S. G. Macdonell, "A baseline model for software effort estimation," ACM TOSEM, vol. 24, no. 3, pp. 20:1-20:11
edges.evidence: Whigham et al. [27] propose guidelines for designing a baseline implementation that include: 1) Be simple to describe and implement; 2) Be applicable to a range of models; 3) Be publicly available

edges.target: No Free Lunch theorems (Wolpert & Macready)
edges.ref: [24] D. H. Wolpert and W. G. Macready, "No free lunch theorems for optimization," Trans. Evol. Comp, vol. 1, no. 1, pp. 67-82, Apr. 1997.
edges.evidence: According to Wolpert & Macready [24], no single algorithm can ever be best for all problems ... Hence, when commissioning a transfer learner for a new domain, there is always the need for some experimentation

edges.target: Holte OneR as baseline scout
edges.ref: [26] R. C. Holte, "Very Simple Classification Rules Perform Well on Most Commonly Used Datasets," Machine Learning, vol. 11, p. 63, 1993.
edges.evidence: Holte [26] uses the OneR baseline algorithm as a scout that runs ahead of a more complicated learners as a way to judge the complexity of up-coming tasks

edges.target: Cohen, Empirical Methods for AI (compare against simpler alternatives)
edges.ref: [25] P. R. Cohen, Empirical Methods for Artificial Intelligence. MIT Press, 1995.
edges.evidence: Cohen [25] strongly recommends comparing supposedly sophisticated systems against simpler alternatives

edges.target: Shepperd & MacDonell: measurements as ratios vs minimal baseline
edges.ref: [29] M. J. Shepperd and S. G. MacDonell, "Evaluating prediction systems in software project estimation," Information & Software Technology, vol. 54
edges.evidence: Shepperd and Macdonnel [29] argue convincingly that measurements are best viewed as ratios compared to measurements taken from some minimal baseline system

edges.target: Zimmermann et al. cross-project defect prediction: 622 pairs, 4% success
edges.ref: [17] T. Zimmermann, N. Nagappan, H. Gall, E. Giger, and B. Murphy, "Cross-project defect prediction: a large scale experiment on data vs. domain vs.
edges.evidence: Zimmermann et al. [17] learned defect predictors from 622 pairs of projects project1, project2. In only 4% of pairs, predictors from project1 worked on project2

edges.target: Turhan: dataset shift / 28 studies with differing conclusions
edges.ref: [93] B. Turhan, "On the dataset shift problem in software engineering prediction models," Empirical Software Engineering, vol. 17, pp. 62-74, 2012.
edges.evidence: Turhan [93] showed that the reason for this inconsistency is due to dataset drift ... (1) Source component shift; (2) Domain Shift; (3) Imbalanced Data

edges.target: Burak filter / cross-vs-within company defect data (Turhan, Menzies et al.)
edges.ref: [15] B. Turhan, T. Menzies, A. B. Bener, and J. Di Stefano, "On the relative value of cross-company and within-company data for defect prediction,"
edges.evidence: training on S = 9 source projects and testing on T = 1 target projects resulted in alarmingly high false positive rates (60% or more) ... the Burak filter suffered from instability

edges.target: Menzies et al. local vs global models SLR (Figure 2 tabulation, cluster-specific models)
edges.ref: [92] T. Menzies, A. Butcher, A. Marcus, T. Zimmermann, and D. Cok, "Local vs. global models for effort estimation and defect prediction," in ASE
edges.evidence: In our previous work, we conducted a large scale systematic literature review [92]. We distilled our findings into a list of 28 studies ... These findings are tabulated in Figure 2

edges.target: Menzies et al. COCOMO coefficient instability (only loc stable)
edges.ref: [94] T. Menzies, Z. Chen, D. Port, and J. Hihn, "Simple software cost estimation: Safe or unsafe?" in Proceedings, PROMISE workshop, ICSE 2005, 2005.
edges.evidence: only the coefficient on lines of code (loc) was stable while the variance in dozens of other coefficients were extremely large ... five coefficients ... changed from positive to negative

edges.target: Jorgensen: 15 studies model-vs-expert split 5/5/5
edges.ref: [95] M. Jorgensen, "Realism in assessment of effort estimation uncertainty: It matters how you ask," IEEE Trans. Softw. Eng., vol. 30, no. 4, pp.
edges.evidence: Jorgensen [95] compared model-based to expert-based methods in 15 different studies ... five studies favored expert-based methods, five found no difference, and five favored model-based methods

edges.target: Kitchenham et al. cross-vs-within company review: 3 of 7 not worse
edges.ref: [96] B. Kitchenham, E. Mendes, and G. H. Travassos, "Cross versus within-company cost estimation studies: A systematic review," IEEE Trans. Softw.
edges.evidence: Of these seven studies, three found that models from other organizations were not significantly worse than those based on local data, while four found that they were significantly worse

edges.target: MacDonell & Shepperd local vs global review: 10 studies
edges.ref: [97] S. G. MacDonell and M. J. Shepperd, "Comparing local and global software effort estimation models - reflections on a systematic review," in ESEM
edges.evidence: From a total of 10 studies, two were found to be inconclusive, three supported global models, and five supported local models

edges.target: Mair & Shepperd regression vs analogy: 20 studies 7/4/9
edges.ref: [98] C. Mair and M. Shepperd, "The consistency of empirical comparisons of regression and analogy-based software project cost prediction," in ESEM
edges.evidence: From a total of 20 empirical studies, (a) seven recommended regression for building effort estimators; (b) four were indifferent; and (c) nine favored analogy

edges.target: Menzies, Greenwald, Frank: defect predictors find 70% of defects
edges.ref: [120] T. Menzies, J. Greenwald, and A. Frank, "Data mining static code attributes to learn defect predictors," IEEE TSE, January 2007.
edges.evidence: defect predictors often find the location of 70% (or more) of the defects in code [120]. Defect predictors have some level of generality: predictors learned at NASA [120] have also been found useful elsewhere

edges.target: IEEE Metrics 2002 panel: manual reviews find ~60% of defects (Shull et al.)
edges.ref: [123] F. Shull, V. Basili, B. Boehm, et al., "What we have learned about fighting defects," in Proc. 8th International Software Metrics Symposium
edges.evidence: a panel at IEEE Metrics 2002 [123] concluded that manual software reviews can find ~60% of defects

edges.target: Rahman et al.: static bug finders vs statistical prediction equally cost-effective
edges.ref: [125] F. Rahman, S. Khatri, E. T. Barr, and P. Devanbu, "Comparing static bug finders and statistical prediction," in Proc. ICSE 2014, pp. 424-434.
edges.evidence: Rahman et al. [125] compared (a) static code analysis tools FindBugs, Jlint, and Pmd and (b) static code defect predictors ... They found no significant differences in the cost-effectiveness

edges.target: Hall et al. SLR: data imbalance linked to poor performance
edges.ref: [66] T. Hall, S. Beecham, D. Bowes, D. Gray, and S. Counsell, "A systematic literature review on fault prediction performance in software
edges.evidence: A systematic literature review on software defect prediction carried out by Hall et al. [66] indicated that data imbalance may be connected to poor performance

edges.target: Fowler et al. bad-smell catalogue (Figure 1 taxonomy, smell definition)
edges.ref: [32] M. Fowler, K. Beck, J. Brant, W. Opdyke, and D. Roberts, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code. Addison-Wesley Longman, 1999.
edges.evidence: the first column lists commonly mentioned bad smells and comes from Fowler's 1999 text [32] ... bad smells (a.k.a. code smells) are "a surface indication that usually corresponds to a deeper problem"

edges.target: Xu et al. 'too many knobs' configuration complexity
edges.ref: [23] T. Xu, L. Jin, X. Fan, Y. Zhou, S. Pasupathy, and R. Talwadker, "Hey, you have given me too many knobs!" in ESEC/FSE 2015, pp. 307-319.
edges.evidence: Xu et al. [23] discuss the cost of increasing software complexity: as complexity increases users use fewer and fewer of the available configuration options

edges.target: Hassan: managers lose faith when analytics results keep changing
edges.ref: [19] A. Hassan, "Remarks made during a presentation to the ucl crest open workshop," March 2017.
edges.evidence: Hassan [19] cautions that managers lose faith in the results of software analytics if those results keep changing

not_reuse_examples: [10]/[11]/[12] Nam & Kim heterogeneous defect prediction and Jing et al. CCA: discussed in Sec 5.1 survey of transfer learning only; heterogeneous transfer not run here (only [10] TCA+ is executed).
[104]-[107] Kreimer, Khomh et al. BDTEX, Yang et al.: code-smell ML detectors explicitly excluded, 'These studies were not included in our comparison as the data was not readily available'.
[110]-[112] Panjer, Giger, Zhang issue-lifetime predictors: background numbers (34.9%, 65% precision) describing the domain, not premises or comparison targets.
[37]-[64] the 28 OO-metric studies in Figure 2 and [81]-[90] data-drift / belief papers: cited as survey evidence of instability, not run or adopted.
[14] Kocaguneli TEAK and [13],[16],[156] relevancy-filtering work: mentioned as prior transfer learners superseded by newer methods; not executed here (compared only in the earlier ASE'16 paper).
notes: Empirical TSE-style journal extension of the authors' ASE'16 bellwether paper (arXiv 1703.06218v4); four SE domains, three prior transfer learners re-implemented as baselines, own replication package (zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.891082); reference list has duplicate entries ([17]=[91], [18]=[92], [29]=[137]=[152], [30]=[96]) and some garbled two-column ref text.
